title: Samatha, calm
hookLine: a bowl of water, stirred, then left still: calm practice steadies the mind on one object

lines: A BOWL OF WATER, A FACE.
STILL WATER, AND THERE IT IS.
cards: In one of the Buddha's discourses, a man leans over a bowl of water to see his own face, and it goes wrong in five ways. The water has dye mixed in. Or it's boiling on a fire.
Or it's grown over with moss. Or wind is rippling the surface. Or it's muddy and set down in the dark.
Each time, the face won't show. Then the water is clear, still, in the light, and there it is. The discourse says a mind works the same way.

teach.b: Samatha is the Pali word for calm, or tranquility: a mind steadied on one object. First, one object. Calm practice picks a single thing and stays with it, often the breath, felt at one spot, the nostrils or the belly.
Each time the mind wanders, it's brought back, gently. Over time it wanders less, and settles.
Second, the five troubles in the water. Each spoiled bowl stands for a hindrance. Dye is sensual craving.
Boiling is ill will. Moss is dullness and drowsiness. Wind is restlessness and worry.
Mud in the dark is doubt. Calm doesn't argue with them; it lets them settle, the way mud sinks when you stop stirring. Third, a pair.
Yesterday was vipassana, insight. In another short discourse, the Buddha names the two together.
Calm, the text says in paraphrase, develops the mind and lets craving fall away; insight develops wisdom and lets ignorance fall away. Partners, not rivals. Fourth, how teachers use them.

teach.h: CALM FIRST, OR INSIGHT FROM THE START.
teach.b: Some have students build calm first, then turn it toward insight. Others begin with insight from the start, using just enough steadiness to look. Both point back to the same pair.
And on an ordinary day, calm is the plain gift of a mind that isn't stirred up: water still enough to see what's in front of you, including yourself.

how: In Theravada practice, calm meditation usually rests attention on a single object such as the breath at the nostrils, returning to it each time the mind wanders, often alongside insight practice.

o: calm: a mind steadied on one object until it settles
the strain of holding on to pleasant feelings
a chant repeated to call on the Buddha for help

s: calm practice means arguing the hindrances away
calm lets them settle, the way mud sinks when you stop stirring.
the Buddha names calm and insight together, as partners
calm develops the mind; insight develops wisdom.
every Theravada teacher builds calm before insight
teachers differ: some build calm first, others begin with insight from the start.

games.q: you're resting on the breath at the nostrils, and your mind wanders to dinner. what does calm practice ask?
o: notice where it went and come back gently.
switch to thinking about the breath instead.
games.why: the coming back is the practice. over time the mind wanders less, and settles, like water.

practice: Choose one spot where the breath is easy to feel, the tip of the nose or the rise and fall of the belly, and stay there, breath after breath, without following it anywhere else.
When the mind wanders, notice where it went and come back without scolding; that coming back is the practice.

wordCard.voice: Samatha. Calm. A mind steadied on one object, until the stirred-up water settles and clears. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: calm, tranquility, a mind steadied on one object.

carryVoice: Your line: calm. Stop stirring, and the water clears. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 46.55 (the bowl of water and the five hindrances)
